reading.body:
A single OpenStreetMap way in Dueville, Italy is tagged as a data center under the name "Set," and nothing in the record identifies who operates it or how much power it draws.

The entry is one point in a global map of data centers, and its value is as a location, not as a capacity figure. The record carries no megawatts, no operator, no website, and no business registration. The name "Set" is a short generic word that could be an abbreviation, an acronym, or a fragment of a longer company name. Dueville sits in the Veneto region near Vicenza, an area of light industry and small technology firms, so a small IT company is plausible, but the data does not confirm it.

For AI specifically, this tells a reader almost nothing. Compute capacity depends on power, cooling, and the buildings that house servers, and none of those quantities appear here. A facility can be tagged on a map and still be a single rack in an office, or a shell with no equipment. The absence of a megawatt value is not evidence of a small facility, only evidence that the source did not record one.

What the data does establish is that OpenStreetMap contributors tag data centers in ordinary Italian towns, not just in the industrial parks and hyperscale corridors that dominate coverage. That matters for anyone counting facilities, because the long tail of small and unconfirmed sites is where a map's totals get soft. The record also shows its own limits: the research note states that search quota was exhausted, so the operator was never confirmed rather than confirmed absent.
